cards.title: Introduction to Logging
cards.content:
Logging is crucial for monitoring the health and behavior of your ASP.NET Core applications. It helps you diagnose issues, audit user actions, and track performance.

ASP.NET Core comes with a built-in, high-performance logging framework that supports multiple logging providers like Console, Debug, EventSource, and third-party tools like Serilog or NLog.

cards.title: Understanding Log Levels
cards.content:
ASP.NET Core defines several log levels in the LogLevel enum, ordered from lowest to highest severity:

  • Trace: Most detailed messages. Usually contain sensitive data.
  • Debug: Short-term diagnostic messages.
  • Information: Tracks the general flow of the application.
  • Warning: Abnormal or unexpected events that don't stop execution.
  • Error: Current flow is stopped due to a failure.
  • Critical: Unrecoverable crashes requiring immediate attention.
  • None: Specifies that a message should not be logged.

options.text: Error is more severe than Critical
Warning is less severe than Error
Information is more severe than Warning
Trace is the highest severity level

cards.title: Using ILogger in Controllers
cards.content:
The standard way to write logs in ASP.NET Core is by injecting the generic ILogger<T> interface into your classes via Dependency Injection.

public class HomeController : Controller
{
    private readonly ILogger<HomeController> _logger;

    public HomeController(ILogger<HomeController> logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }

    public IActionResult Index()
    {
        _logger.LogInformation("Index page visited at {Time}", DateTime.UtcNow);
        return View();
    }
}

cards.title: Structured Logging & Message Templates
cards.content:
ASP.NET Core supports structured logging. Instead of string concatenation (e.g., "User " + id + " logged in"), use message templates with named placeholders.

_logger.LogInformation("User {UserId} logged in from {IpAddress}", userId, ipAddress);

This allows logging providers to index parameters separately, making it easier to query logs in systems like Elasticsearch or Application Insights.

cards.title: Configuring Logging in appsettings.json
cards.content:
You can configure minimum log levels and provider-specific settings in appsettings.json under the Logging section:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"
    }
  }
}

This configuration sets the global default level to Information, while restricting ASP.NET Core internal framework logs to Warning and above.

cards.title: Logging Best Practices Summary
cards.content:
To wrap up, keep these best practices in mind:

  • Use appropriate log levels (don't log everything as Error).
  • Leverage structured logging instead of string interpolation.
  • Avoid logging sensitive data (PII, passwords, connection strings).
  • Configure appropriate filtering in production to avoid log bloat.
